title: The Contract Is the Beginning
text: Winning a contract is not the finish line. It is the moment someone decides to trust you.
bodyHtml:
Over the past few months, I’ve been reflecting on the beliefs that have quietly shaped how I work—through customers, colleagues, leadership, and more than a few mistakes along the way.

Here’s one I’ve kept coming back to.

Early in my career, I thought customers remembered the best presentation.

Or the most competitive price.

Or even the project we delivered.

I don’t think that’s true anymore.

I’ve come to believe customers remember something much simpler.

Winning a contract wasn’t the finish line.

It was simply the moment someone decided to trust us.

The real work started after the signatures.

Would we deliver?

Would we communicate honestly when something didn’t go according to plan?

Would we stay engaged long after the project was complete?

Over the years, one question quietly became my guide.

Can I become one less thing my customer has to worry about?

Not the cheapest supplier.

Not the smartest person in the room.

Just one less thing they had to worry about.

Looking back, I think that’s where the strongest relationships came from.

Because people knew I would take ownership, communicate honestly, and stay with the problem until it was resolved.

I’ve realised that this applies far beyond customers.

It applies to colleagues.

To partnerships.

To leadership.

Relationships often outlast the projects that brought people together.

Customers may forget the presentation, the proposal, or even parts of the project.

They rarely forget how you made them feel when things became difficult.

That’s a lesson I’m still trying to live up to every day.

title: The Most Important Thing You Negotiate Isn't the Contract
text: The best negotiation is not the one you win. It is the one that leaves a relationship worth continuing.
bodyHtml:
One of my former bosses used to say something I've never forgotten.

If you lose $10,000 on a job because you can't collect it, you'll need another $100,000 job just to recover that loss.

He was talking about protecting margins.

For years, I thought that was the lesson.

Looking back, I think there was another one hidden inside it.

Every meaningful negotiation represents months, sometimes years, of conversations, meetings, presentations, follow-ups, and gradually, trust.

By the time two people sit down to discuss the final terms, they've already started building something far more valuable than a commercial agreement.

They've already started building a relationship.

That's why I've never believed a negotiation ends when both parties sign the dotted line.

I think that's where it begins.

Early in my career, I judged every negotiation by one question:

Did we get the deal?

Over time, that question changed.

Today, I ask myself something different.

Did we build a relationship worth continuing?

I've never wanted to win the negotiation if it meant losing the relationship.

But there's a difference between negotiating firmly and negotiating in a way that leaves the other person hoping they never have to work with you again.

Growing up in India, I often heard the saying:

The operation was successful, but the patient died.

Sometimes I think the same can happen in business.

You can negotiate the perfect contract.

Walk away believing you won.

But if the relationship ends there, what have you really achieved?

During one of our negotiation exercises at UCLA Anderson, the objective wasn't simply to maximise the outcome.

We were expected to leave the negotiation in a way that preserved the relationship, even if no agreement was reached.

That resonated with me.

It reinforced something I had been learning throughout my career: sometimes the next opportunity is more valuable than winning the current negotiation.

Today, when I think about the negotiations I'm most proud of, I rarely remember the final commercial terms.

I remember the people.

The conversations that continued.

The customers who called again.

Because it takes months, sometimes years, to earn the opportunity to sit across the table from someone.

I've never wanted to waste that opportunity over one more concession.

That's a lesson I'm still trying to live up to every day.

title: Relationships Are Built by Working Together
text: Shared work creates stronger relationships than introductions ever could.
bodyHtml:
One of the most overused words in business school is networking.

I’ve never been completely comfortable with that word.

It can sound transactional, as if the goal is simply to collect contacts.

Over the last two years at UCLA Anderson, I’ve come to appreciate something different.

Relationships are built by working together.

Some of my most meaningful connections came through study groups. Others came through the LMI Sand Prize, the Ethics Summit, the HPE competition, the Social Impact Consulting Corps, activities, and countless conversations outside the classroom.

A few of those efforts resulted in recognition. But the awards were never the point.

The real value was the opportunity to work with people from different industries, backgrounds, experiences, and ways of thinking.

Every project taught me something.

Every team challenged my assumptions.

Every collaboration expanded my perspective.

Looking back, one of the best decisions I made was saying “yes” to opportunities that allowed me to work with people beyond my immediate circle.

These shared experiences created stronger connections than introductions ever could.

I’m glad I said yes to projects, competitions, and teams outside my comfort zone.

Many of the experiences I remember most started as opportunities I almost passed on.

And if there’s one lesson I’ll carry forward, it’s that some of the most valuable learning happens while building something together.

title: Curiosity Keeps You in the Game
text: The real risk is not being wrong. It is assuming the game has stopped moving.
bodyHtml:
Here’s a fascinating truth in sports:

The moment you think you’ve mastered the game is often the moment you start falling behind.

Not because your performance drops.

But because the baseline of excellence keeps moving forward.

That idea has stayed with me.

After many years in industry, I came to UCLA Anderson expecting most of my learning to come from new frameworks and tools.

Instead, some of the most meaningful growth has come from deliberately walking into rooms where I wasn’t the most familiar with the subject.

Over the past two years, I’ve worked alongside medical, law, and public policy students across sustainability initiatives, nonprofit consulting projects, and much more.

What stood out wasn’t just the difference in how people think, but how openly they shared what they knew while remaining equally curious about perspectives outside their own field.

That combination is rare. And powerful.

To push myself further, I also joined cross-campus, cross-disciplinary experiences, marketing and ethics case competitions, and nonprofit consulting projects.

One of the unique things about UCLA is the range of experiences it enables across disciplines.

Months later, those teams are still working together, continuing to learn and take on new challenges.

That, more than anything, has reinforced the value of cross-boundary collaboration.

UCLA legend John Wooden said success is the peace of mind that comes from knowing you gave your absolute best.

That idea is liberating.

It removes the pressure of always needing to have all the answers.

And replaces it with something more valuable: curiosity.

In the long run, the real risk isn’t being wrong. It’s assuming the game stops moving.

title: Focus on the Gaps
text: Strong systems do not fail only at the big rocks. They fail where small gaps are ignored.
bodyHtml:
The squirrel and the bridge.

Armies are moving massive stones.

The vision is bold. The structure is ambitious.

In the middle of all this, a small squirrel keeps carrying tiny pebbles, one at a time.

Ever wondered what the squirrel is doing there?

I used to open my presentations with this image.

I’d tell them:

You’re doing the hard, visible work—designing complex systems. I’m not here to redesign the bridge or challenge the vision.

I’m here to focus on the gaps.

Because bridges don’t fail where the biggest rocks are placed.

They fail where the small gaps are ignored.

Those gaps look minor.

Until stress hits.

Until compliance is tested.

Until what looked right on paper meets the reality of the field.

In high-stakes environments, this mindset isn’t optional.

It’s the difference between a system that appears strong and one that actually holds.

I’ve chosen to do the work that protects what others build.

To strengthen systems before they’re tested.

One pebble at a time.
